user_query: Caller seems vulnerable — how do I assess this and adapt my response?
variations: Caller says a social worker told them to call.
Caller has a disability that affects their ability to seek help.
part_a_general_info: Vulnerability affects (a) how you conduct the call (pace, language, patience) and (b) which scheme pathway is appropriate. You do NOT ask the caller directly "are you vulnerable?" — you assess from cues and, where natural, use the sensitively-worded probes in Part B. If two or more factors are present, or any single severe factor (e.g., minor, ongoing violence, FSC-referred), treat as HIGH-vulnerability and escalate. Vulnerability factors to listen for: • Violence victim (current or recent) • Elderly caller with apparent confusion or isolation • Technology-illiterate (cannot use email, apps, online forms) • Language barrier (limited English and no other listed language handled) • Minor (under 18) • Already engaged with an FSC social worker • Basic needs at risk (food, shelter, money) • Physical or cognitive disability affecting independent action Scheme implications: vulnerable callers may qualify for the Community Law Centre (free legal consultation, usually by in-house team who can provide greater support). High-vulnerability cases should be escalated to PBSG Staff (Route F of GEN3-T01) for hand-holding.
triage_questions: Q1: "To make sure I understand your situation — are you speaking for yourself today, or did someone help you make this call?" (Probes: caregiver involvement, third-party influence, language assistance.)
Q2: "Is there anything about how we're speaking today that would make it easier for you — for example, would you prefer a different language, or should I speak more slowly?"
Q3: "Are you currently safe where you are, and do you have a safe place to stay tonight?"
Q4: "Are you currently working with a social worker, counsellor, or case officer on anything?"
Q5: "Can I just check — are you 18 or older?" (Only ask if age is genuinely unclear. Do not ask callers who are obviously adult.)
Q6: "Is there anything I should know that would help me help you better — any health, mobility, or access concerns?"
branching_logic: Q1: "To make sure I understand your situation — are you speaking for yourself today, or did someone help you make this call?" (Probes: caregiver involvement, third-party influence, language assistance.)
If caller indicates a helper is present → note who; ask permission to continue with caller directly.
Q2: "Is there anything about how we're speaking today that would make it easier for you — for example, would you prefer a different language, or should I speak more slowly?"
Record language preference. If not one PBSG handles, note for escalation to interpreter.
Q3: "Are you currently safe where you are, and do you have a safe place to stay tonight?"
If No or unclear → cross-reference GEN3-T06 (Urgent Matter) Route A/B.
Q4: "Are you currently working with a social worker, counsellor, or case officer on anything?"
If Yes → ask for the FSC or organisation name; treat as HIGH-vulnerability; coordinate rather than duplicate.
Q5: "Can I just check — are you 18 or older?" (Only ask if age is genuinely unclear. Do not ask callers who are obviously adult.)
If caller is under 18 → Route B (Minor — Special Handling).
Q6: "Is there anything I should know that would help me help you better — any health, mobility, or access concerns?"
Note any disclosed disability or accessibility need.
If ≥2 vulnerability cues detected OR any severe single factor (minor, active violence, FSC-referred) → Route A (High-Vulnerability — Escalate + Community Law Centre).
If 1 cue, non-severe → Route C (Low-Vulnerability — Standard Triage with Adaptations).
If unclear/uncertain → Route A (Escalate to PBSG Staff for professional assessment).
routing: Route A (High-Vulnerability — Escalate + Community Law Centre):
Route C (Low-Vulnerability — Standard Triage with Adaptations):
guardrail: • Under s 33 of the Legal Profession Act 1966, only qualified, practising lawyers may give legal advice. You must NEVER: (a) interpret a legal document for the caller; (b) apply the law to the caller's facts; (c) predict the outcome of a case; (d) tell the caller what they should do legally. • You MAY: (a) confirm scheme eligibility against objective criteria; (b) read out scheme descriptions verbatim; (c) explain PBSG hotline operations; (d) take down particulars and escalate to PBSG Staff. • If the caller insists on legal advice, respond: “I’m an intern/volunteer and I’m not able to give legal advice. What I can do is help you find the right legal help avenue or direct you to a qualified lawyer.” • If in doubt at any point — escalate to PBSG Staff. • Protect caller confidentiality. Do not discuss the caller outside the hotline context. Do not retain personal data on personal devices and/or beyond the PBSG volunteering period.
